Saudi plans Houthi offensive with 100,000 Yemeni troops, US, other countries' support
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/YEMEN

Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.

The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will by led by Yemeni forces on the ground, which are overseen by Riyadh, and supported by Saudi air strikes, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations.

While the US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, and some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, the Saudi allies aren't expected to play a direct role in combat operations, said the people who requested anonymity to discuss security matters.

Saudi Arabia entered neighbouring Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognised government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

A key objective of the planned Saudi offensive, which hasn't been previously reported, is aimed at reversing the rapid gains made by the Houthis last month when they advanced down the coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, according to the people with knowledge of the plans who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.

The Saudis are considering two possible options for the assault, the Gulf and Yemeni officials said: Either a narrowly focused attack on the area around Bab el-Mandeb or a broader offensive that also includes other synchronized attacks on multiple fronts around Yemen, in the governorates of Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.

More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, the officials all said.

Spokespeople for the Saudi and Yemeni governments, the Houthi group and the US military didn't immediately respond to requests for comment about the Saudi plans.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that's assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.

Riyadh has concluded it cannot enter new Yemeni peace negotiations with the Houthis while the militants remain in control of Bab el-Mandeb, giving them significant global leverage, the Western diplomats and Gulf official said.

The six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations couldn't give a precise timing for the launch of the offensive, with their estimates ranging from within a week to until after the US midterm elections in early November.

Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected an offensive to be narrowly focused and certainly more modest in scope than the Saudi-led operation in 2015 that sought to rout the militants.

"As much they want to vanquish the Houthis completely, they also need to get back to status quo ante before Houthis controlled territory along Bab el-Mandeb," he added. "Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic."

The Houthis have become Iran's most formidable ally in the Middle East since Israel's degradation of Hezbollah in Lebanon over the past three years.

A Saudi-directed offensive against the group would mark a new flashpoint in a region engulfed by conflict since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel of 7 October 2023 and the subsequent US-Israeli war on Iran.

Trump, Turkey and Pakistan

Washington, Saudi Arabia's most powerful ally, is providing military advisers and intelligence including targeting information to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to one of the Western diplomats.

However, the extent of support may be limited. Reuters has previously reported that US President Donald Trump rebuffed requests by the de facto Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman for direct military support such as air strikes.

Turkey and Pakistan, with whom Saudi Arabia signed a joint defence agreement last month, have provided military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen, Pakistani and regional officials said.

Last month, Pakistan sent four cargo planes with equipment including air defence systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone systems to Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, a Pakistani government official said.

Pakistani military advisers are also on the ground with Saudi counterparts to support Yemeni forces, according to a second Pakistani official, the Gulf official and a Western diplomat. Turkish drones, bought by Saudi Arabia before the current war, have also been deployed over Yemen, they added.

One of the kingdom's key concerns in launching a new offensive in Yemen is how to protect its oil facilities and other infrastructure from Houthi drone and missile attacks, according to regional officials who said Riyadh has asked several allies for help with defensive systems.

Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's land borders and help with drone and missile interceptions, according to the second Pakistani official, who said the troops arrived in waves beginning last year but also after the recent escalation. Islamabad hasn't made any decision to send troops into Yemen in a fighting capacity, the official said.

The Pakistani and Turkish defence ministries didn't respond to requests for comment on their military support for Riyadh.

France, meanwhile, has announced it will send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Fractured Yemeni forces

Any ground operation inside Yemen will rely on the disparate coalition of Yemeni fighting factions that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates armed and trained at earlier stages of the civil war when the conflict ground to a bloody stalemate.

"Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organised or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force. And they are being tested right now, as the Houthis apply pressure across several fronts at once," said Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha.

Yemeni forces were further fractured last winter when southern fighters backed by the UAE tried to take territory in the east and announce secession plans, leading to their defeat by Saudi-backed fighters after a series of clashes.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, cautioned the outcome of any offensive by the Saudis against the Houthis would depend on how ground forces perform.

"The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive," he said. "Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces."

PM Tarique inaugurates fifth Bay of Bengal Conversation
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday inaugurated the fifth edition of the international forum "Bay of Bengal Conversation 2026", bringing together policymakers, diplomats, researchers and experts from over 100 countries.
The three-day conference, organised by the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS), is being held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka from October 3 to 5.
The prime minister formally opened the three-day event around 10am with his address to the opening session.
More than 200 speakers, over 300 delegates and more than 1,000 participants are expected to attend the forum, including former and current heads of state and government, ministers, diplomats, military experts, academics, researchers, journalists, business and investment leaders, human rights defenders, technology specialists and representatives of international development organisations.
Former Serbian President Boris Tadić and former Malian Prime Minister Moussa Mara are among the notable participants.
The theme of this year’s conference is “Fragments, Frontiers and Futures”, with the tagline “Navigating Power, Technology and Trust in a World Rewritten.”
The discussions will focus on major regional and global issues, including geopolitics and security, technology, trade and connectivity, climate change, human security, democracy, governance, trust, spirituality and humanity.
CGS President Zillur Rahman and Executive Director Parvez Karim Abbasi delivered the welcome remarks at the opening of the conference.
Zillur Rahman said the Bay of Bengal is becoming increasingly important in the context of maritime security and regional geopolitics.
“As a vital link between South Asia and Southeast Asia, one of the key objectives of this initiative is to explore effective solutions to the challenges and opportunities rooted in the Bay,” he said.
He said this year’s discussions would focus on geopolitics, security, trust, climate change, spirituality and humanity.
The program includes public sessions such as plenaries, leadership forums and spotlight talks, as well as smaller invitation-only roundtables for in-depth discussions, according to the organisers.

item.title: UK maritime agency: Oil tankers attacked in Hormuz strait
item.description:
Two oil tankers have been struck by "unidentified projectiles" in the Strait of Hormuz region, a British maritime agency said Friday, in the latest threat to shipping in the waterway.
The Hormuz passage, through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG passed before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February and sparked the Middle East war, remains at the heart of the conflict.
Tehran has been blocking the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorised crossings.
Washington responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Tehran from exporting its oil.
The first attack caused "a small fire and blackout onboard", the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said Friday, adding that the fire was later extinguished.
There were no reported casualties or environmental impact, it added.
The vessel, which was exiting the strait, was able to resume its journey, UKMTO said, without specifying the ship's ports of origin and destination.
Hours later, another crude oil tanker reported being struck by an "unknown projectile" east of Oman, with all crew safe and no environmental damage reported, according to the UKMTO.
The agency said authorities were investigating the incidents.

item.title: Uranium consignment reaches Rooppur nuclear power plant amid tight security
item.description:
A uranium consignment for the second unit of Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant reached the project site in Pabna on Saturday afternoon amid tight security.
Three uranium-laden lorries arrived at the nuclear power plant site around 12:25pm after leaving Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 7:15am under the security escort of the Bangladesh Army, said Pabna Deputy Commissioner Aminul Islam.
The consignment is the first shipment of uranium for the second unit of the Rooppur plant.
A special cargo aircraft carrying the uranium landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at around 11:44pm on Friday.
After completing the necessary formalities, the uranium was transported to Rooppur in three lorries while another vehicle carried other equipment.
A team of specialists who had arrived from Russia also accompanied the consignment.
Members of the Bangladesh Army, police and various intelligence agencies were deployed to ensure security during the transportation.
The flight carrying uranium for Rooppur plant was scheduled to arrive on September 24 but was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace.
According to project officials, a total of nine uranium consignments are scheduled to be brought to Bangladesh — seven for the second unit and two for the refuelling of the first unit.
All the consignments are scheduled to be delivered by December.
Fuel for the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant was brought to Bangladesh in 2023.
The Rooppur plant, comprising two 1,200-megawatt units, has a total generation capacity of 2,400MW.
Construction of the plant began in 2013 with Russian assistance at an estimated cost of more than Tk1.13 lakh crore.
Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL) Managing Director Dr Zahidul Hasan said testing of the 16-megawatt high-pressure system under the reactor protection and safety-related system was successfully completed on Wednesday following the replacement of a defective valve.

item.title: With Russia next door and rising costs, Latvia goes to the polls
item.description:
Latvia will vote Saturday in an election shaped by concerns over neighboring Russia and the cost of living, but the result is not expected to steer the country off its pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
The center-right United List party of incumbent Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs is at the head of the race, with over 14% of the vote, according to the SKDS institute.
His coalition, however, is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain ground by focusing on economic concerns in the least affluent of the three Baltic states.
The current governing coalition is made up of United List, New Unity, the Union of Greens and Farmers, and the National Alliance. Polls suggest the bloc is unlikely to retain power in its current form after the vote.
Criticized as pro-Russian by its detractors, the populist Sovereign Power party, led by Julija Stepanenko, is polling at over nine percent and could become the second-largest party in Latvia’s 100-seat unicameral parliament.
The party has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases to defense spending, instead highlighting domestic economic problems.
Despite its gains, the party is unlikely to enter government because most major parties have ruled out cooperation with it.
Another populist force, Latvia First, led by businessman Ainars Slesers, could prove a more viable coalition partner.
The Progressives, a pro-European social democratic party advocating stronger social protections and continued support for Ukraine, are polling around six percent.
With roughly one in five voters still undecided, the final composition of the next parliament remains uncertain. Fourteen electoral lists are contesting the election, but polls indicate only seven are likely to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament.
Security remains central to political debate four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Latvia, a member of Nato and the European Union since 2004, views Russia as its principal security threat and has significantly increased defense spending in response.
It has sharply increased its defense spending since Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Kyiv, now allocating nearly five percent of its GDP to defense.
Most parties expected to enter parliament support maintaining military spending at elevated levels and continuing assistance to Kyiv.
Economic issues nevertheless remain crucial to voters. Rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline all feature prominently in campaign debates.
Voting patterns among Latvia’s large Russian-speaking minority are also changing.
Once concentrated behind the Harmony party, which lost parliamentary representation in 2022, many voters are increasingly making choices based on economic and social issues rather than identity politics alone.
Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.
Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.
Exit polls are expected shortly after polling stations close.

item.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile after Seoul’s apology demand
item.description:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile, Seoul’s military said Saturday, days after demanding an apology for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ that it blames on the North.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month’s explosion inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) and called South Korea “despicable” on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul’s civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue.
Early Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
“South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defense posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometers (435 miles).
Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month’s explosion inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice, was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.
North Korea’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un’s designation of South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy” in 2024.
The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work, according to South Korea’s defense minister Kang Shin-chul.
South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
She ridiculed Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch” and said the military’s demand her country apologize was “quite ridiculous.”
Kim also warned Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast -- remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government’s diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.
“Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
“The message is that the North is pursuing... confrontation in response to goodwill,” he added.
South Korea’s defense minister said on Tuesday the military had “a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages” to respond to the DMZ incident, without providing further detail.
The South’s Unification Minister, Chung Dong-young, also proposed talks to address issues along the border to Pyongyang on Friday.
Kim Yo Jong, however, dismissed Chung’s suggestion of talks as a “wild dream and unilateral jargon.”
The flare-up comes at a sensitive time when US President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that Seoul -- an ally of Washington -- could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
South Korea’s opposition People Power Party on Friday accused Lee of failing to criticize Pyongyang when warranted even as he takes a hard line on Ukraine for publicly disclosing the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war, an arrangement Seoul believed should be confidential.
“South Korean soldiers have been injured, and far from receiving an apology, we have been mocked by North Korea,” the opposition party said in a statement.
“We fail to see how selectively turning a blind eye to North Korea serves South Korea’s dignity or the safety of its people.”

Dinesh Trivedi stresses dialogue, trust to address Dhaka-Delhi issues
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Saturday highlighted the need for continuous dialogue, mutual respect and trust between the two countries to address bilateral issues, saying every issue between the two neighbors has a solution.
“There’s no point hiding the issues, and there’s no point not talking about the issues,” he said while speaking at a discussion titled “Power and Prudence: Managing Great-Power Competition without Conflict” as part of the ongoing Bay of Bengal Conversation in Dhaka.
Trivedi, who faced a couple of questions, said the two countries need to discuss all outstanding issues, including water, trade, culture, sports, communication and transportation, through appropriate forums.
“In a democracy, the dialogue has to be there at the proper forum. And the dialogue has to be a continuous dialogue,” he said, noting that the process of engagement between the two countries may be slow, but it has not stopped.
“I can guarantee you, there is no stoppage of process. The process is ongoing,” Trivedi said. “Believe me, there has to be a solution, and there will be a solution,” the Indian diplomat added.
The High Commissioner said Bangladesh as an independent and sovereign country, understands its own security interests and has the right to make its own decisions.
“Bangladesh is an absolutely independent country and people have elected democratically. So whatever decision Bangladesh takes is the decision of Bangladesh government,” he said, adding that “Nobody should tell Bangladesh what they should do.”
Trivedi also said India’s relationship with Bangladesh does not depend on Dhaka’s relations with other countries.
“As far as we are concerned in India, the relationship doesn’t depend on what relation Bangladesh has with other countries,” he said. He stressed that both countries have the right to protect their respective national interests.
“They are absolutely in their very much right to protect their very interest of the peoples. So are we,” Trivedi said.
Describing Bangladesh-India ties as distinct from a merely transactional relationship, he said the two countries share deep cultural and historical bonds.
“We go through not only transactional relationship; it is much beyond which is cultural. And that cultural bond is very, very foundationally solid,” he said.
Trivedi, who said he comes from India’s eastern state of West Bengal, said he understands the historical and cultural connections between the people of the two countries.
“This relationship is very difficult for the outside world to understand, which is culturally deep-rooted,” he said.
He said the two countries’ relationship has a unique cultural foundation, referring to the shared legacy of Bengali cultural icons.
“Can you imagine that one person, Rabindranath Tagore, has written the national anthem for both the countries?” the envoy said.
The High Commissioner also said good neighbors should support each other when faced with calamities or security challenges, while respecting each other’s sovereignty and domestic policies. “At the same time, no neighbor has any reason to interfere in each other’s policies,” he said.
Trivedi acknowledged that disagreements are inevitable between neighboring democracies.
“In a family, there are hiccups, and if I say that no, there are no issues. If there are no issues, there is not democracy. In democracies, you are bound to have issues,” he said.
He said such issues can only be addressed through dialogue and consultation, with trust serving as their foundation.
“Issues can only and only be settled through dialogue, through consultation. And the basis of that dialogue is trust,” he said.
“Without dialogue, it is not possible to sort out relationship from remote. And that is what we feel that is work in progress all the time,” he added.
Trivedi expressed confidence that the strong people-to-people ties between the two countries would continue to underpin bilateral relations. “I have full confidence that it’s here to stay,” he said.
The discussion was organized to examine ways of managing strategic rivalry and reducing the risk of escalation amid growing geopolitical uncertainty.
President of the Bangladesh Institute of Peace and Security Studies Maj Gen (Retd) ANM Muniruzzaman, former Army Commander of the Indian Army Arun Kumar Sahni, Professor at Georgetown University Carol Christine Fair, and foreign relations adviser to the mayor of Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality Mustafa Osman Turan also participated in the discussion.
Managing Director of Cnsltng-Bsnss-Dvlpmnt, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Faris Hadrovic moderated the session.
Turan, who also served as Turkish Ambassador to Bangladesh, said strategic autonomy does not simply mean sitting in the middle.
“It means having the ability to make your own decisions in pursuit of your strategic interests,” he said.
Muniruzzaman said they live in an “extremely contested and fragmented” world and Bangladesh is playing the role of an aspiring middle power.
Arun Kumar Sahni said stability rests on two foundations - sovereignty from a military perspective, and trust.

item.title: PM Tarique shares photo with Trump from New York dinner
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday shared a photo of himself and his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman with US President Donald Trump from a dinner hosted by the US president for world leaders attending the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
The prime minister shared the photo on his Facebook page after the White House released it, showing him and Dr Zubaida Rahman with President Trump.
Trump and First Lady Melania Trump hosted the dinner on September 22 night at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel in New York for heads of state and government of UN member states and their spouses.
The dinner was held in honor of world leaders who had gathered in New York to attend the 81st session of the UNGA.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Dr Zubaida Rahman attended the dinner along with other world leaders and their spouses.
Earlier, the Prime Minister and his wife attended a breakfast hosted by UN Secretary-General António Guterres for heads of state and government and their spouses.
The White House also shared another photo featuring Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and US First Lady Melania Trump during a special meeting of first ladies in New York.
The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, bringing together spouses of heads of state and government from different countries.
During the meeting, Melania Trump unveiled her global children’s welfare initiative, “Fostering the Future Together”, and called on first ladies from other countries to join the initiative.
The Prime Minister went to New York on September 21 – leading a 35-member delegation – to attend the UNGA and delivered his maiden address as Prime Minister at the General Debate on September 24.
He returned home on September 27 morning after wrapping up his five-day visit to the United States.

item.title: DMP commissioner: Gulistan, Fulbaria bus terminals to shift within 3 months
item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed has said the Gulistan and Fulbaria bus terminals in the capital will be relocated to Chunkutia in Keraniganj within 3 months.
He made the remarks while speaking to journalists after inspecting traffic management development activities at the Mohakhali terminal on Saturday.
The DMP commissioner said 10 acres of land would be provided at the Jhilmil project in Chunkutia for use as a depot.
“Jhilmil has already given us permission, and we have started work on the depot there,” he said.
The DMP commissioner said around 75 more acres of land would be available there through the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (Rajuk).
A permanent terminal and depot will be established on the land. There are plans to relocate all transport vehicles and trucks serving 19 districts in the southern region, along with trucks from the Badamtali wholesale market.
Asked how long the process would take, he said: “We have set a maximum timeframe of 3 months. We hope the work will be completed within these 3 months. As soon as the work is completed, the buses from Fulbaria and Gulistan will be shifted there.”
Regarding traffic management at the Mohakhali terminal, the DMP commissioner said: “This will operate under a disciplined system. If anyone attempts even minor irregularities, we will take strict legal action.”
At the event, Member of Parliament Md Shamsur Rahman Simul Biswas said: “We are all frustrated with the intolerable traffic congestion in Dhaka city and the disorder in the road transport sector. We want to change this situation.”

item.title: BB expands export pre-shipment refinance fund to Tk7,000cr
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has expanded its pre-shipment credit refinance facility for export-oriented industries from Tk5,000 crore to Tk7,000 crore, while raising the maximum customer-level interest rate on new loans from 5% to 6%.
The central bank announced the decision in a circular issued by its Banking Regulation and Policy Department-1 on Thursday, stating that the measure aims to sustain export operations and bolster foreign exchange earnings amid economic realities.
To facilitate the expansion, the central bank reallocated Tk2,000 crore from its Tk10,000-crore Export Facilitation Pre-finance Fund (EFPF) into the pre-shipment scheme, bringing the remaining balance of the EFPF down to Tk3,000 crore.
Under the revised structure, participating commercial banks can charge end borrowers a maximum interest rate of 6% per annum.
Correspondingly, the refinancing rate charged by Bangladesh Bank to participating institutions has been raised to 3% from the previous 2%, maintaining a 3% margin for the intermediary banks.

item.title: Russia warns diplomats to leave Kyiv over new strikes threat
item.description:
Russia on Saturday issued a new call for diplomats and foreigners to leave Kyiv, warning the Ukrainian capital of new “massive” air attacks hours after striking another major bridge in the city.
Moscow has ramped up its pummeling of Kyiv, launching waves of drones at the city, targeting key infrastructure and putting the capital on a near-constant state of alert against attacks.
The strike on the Northern Bridge on Saturday morning wounded two people and damaged road surface and trolleybus overhead wires restricting traffic, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
AFP reporters saw traces of an explosion on a pedestrian walkway and technicians repairing power lines on the bridge.
Hours after the attack, the Russian authorities warned of more strikes, issuing a fresh call for diplomats and foreigners to leave the city and refrain from visiting Ukraine.
“We note with concern that not everyone has heeded these warnings, and that individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger,” the Russian foreign ministry said in a statement.
The Russian ministry also stated that “responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning.”
Moscow issued a similar warning in May but heads of state and governments from countries backing Ukraine have defied it by travelling to the war-torn country and the capital in show of support.
On Friday, Klitschko said the city was in a “very dramatic situation” and should now be on a war footing as the enemy was “tearing Kyiv apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.
Kyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, with the attacks and alerts disrupting daily life and sowing traffic chaos.
Long lines of stationary cars and buses clogged major roads on Friday as commuters sought alternate routes, with some forced to continue their journeys on foot.
Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats sound almost round the clock, urging the city’s estimated three million people to seek shelter.
Strikes across the country in recent days have also caused power outages in several regions in the east, north and center, with grid operator Ukrenergo urging consumers to limit usage even as demand increases with colder weather.
Ukraine braces for another difficult winter. Last year, heating and power were cut for days on end as temperatures plunged to -20°C.
The grinding war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has turned into Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
Ukraine has appeared to stabilize the front in recent months, but depleted air-defense stocks since the start of the US-Israeli war in Iran have left its cities exposed to Russian barrages.
The US-brokered peace efforts are effectively frozen as Moscow has shown no signs of dropping its maximalist conditions to end the war, including a demand that Ukraine cede territory in the east that Russia’s troops have not captured.

item.title: Loud explosions heard in Yemen capital
item.description:
Loud explosions were heard in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Saturday, as the Houthis reported airstrikes in the area by Saudi forces.
One correspondent heard at least five blasts in different areas, while another saw two warplanes firing missiles on the city.
Al-Masirah TV, a Houthi-affiliated media outlet, reported “Saudi aggression” against the capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
The channel had also earlier on Saturday reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in the northwestern governorate of Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July, the Houthis claimed.
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is backed by neighboring Saudi Arabia.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east -- a region that is larger but less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after fours years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorization from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive which saw them seize control of coastal regions along the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
Fighting in recent days has centered on Taiz, where 80 combatants in the conflict were reported dead on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday that Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.

item.title: Dengue cases up 74%, deaths 27% from last year
item.description:
Dengue hospitalizations in Bangladesh have surged by nearly 74% compared with the same period last year, with the outbreak accelerating dramatically in September and showing little sign of easing in the first three days of October.
A total of 84,369 dengue patients were hospitalized between January 1 and October 3 this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Compared with 48,491 hospitalizations during the corresponding period last year, as cited in the data reviewed by Dhaka Tribune, this represents 35,878 additional patients, a year-on-year increase of about 74%.
Deaths have also risen substantially. The toll stood at 256 as of Saturday, against 202 by October 3 last year -- an increase of 54 deaths, or nearly 27%.
Behind the year-on-year jump is a steep deterioration since the beginning of the monsoon, culminating in September, when the country recorded by far its highest monthly caseload and death toll of 2026.
September alone accounted for 43,774 hospitalizations and 148 deaths, meaning more than half of all dengue patients hospitalized this year and nearly 58% of the fatalities were recorded in a single month.
And October has begun with little respite.
In just the first three days of the month, another 4,749 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals and 11 died, pushing the cumulative figures from 79,620 hospitalizations and 245 deaths at the end of September to 84,369 and 256 respectively.
The month-by-month figures illustrate how rapidly the outbreak has escalated.
In June, 2,907 dengue patients were hospitalized and 13 died. July saw admissions more than triple to 9,206, with 36 deaths.
The situation worsened sharply in August, when 20,536 patients were hospitalized and 43 died.
Then came September.
Hospitalizations more than doubled from August to 43,774, while deaths jumped from 43 to 148, more than three times the previous month’s toll.
The trajectory has continued into October.
In the latest 24-hour reporting period alone, six people died and another 1,608 were hospitalized across the country.
Two of the deaths occurred in Dhaka South City Corporation and two in Rajshahi division, while Khulna and Barisal divisions recorded one each.
Of the new patients, Chittagong recorded the highest number outside the capital with 319 admissions, followed by Khulna with 276 and Barisal with 215.
Hospitals in Dhaka North City Corporation admitted 171 patients and those in Dhaka South 223, while another 131 were admitted elsewhere in Dhaka division.
Rajshahi recorded 132 new patients, Mymensingh 79 and Rangpur 62.
As of Saturday, 5,631 dengue patients remained under treatment in hospitals across the country, while 78,482 of those admitted this year had been discharged.
Entomologist Prof Dr Kabirul Bashar said the continuing rise showed why mosquito-control programs cannot depend primarily on fogging or killing adult Aedes mosquitoes.
Killing adult mosquitoes provides only temporary relief if eggs and larvae remain in breeding sites, allowing another generation to emerge, he said.
Construction sites have become major breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes, according to Bashar, who stressed the need to hold building owners and construction companies accountable for eliminating stagnant water.
Effective control, he said, requires several measures to operate simultaneously, destroying larvae, removing stagnant water, managing the surrounding environment and maintaining public awareness.
Sporadic drives launched when dengue infections begin rising cannot deliver sustainable results, he warned.
Instead, mosquito control has to continue throughout the year, including during winter when Aedes prevalence is relatively low and authorities have a better opportunity to suppress mosquito populations before the next transmission season.
In practice, however, mosquito-control activities often become less intensive during that period, he said.
With the patient load rising, the government is also strengthening clinical preparedness outside major hospitals.
State Minister for Health Dr MA Muhit said 1,600 doctors across 40 districts were receiving specialized training in dengue clinical management.
Around 350 senior physicians had previously undergone training-of-trainers sessions and were now training other doctors across the districts.
Muhit said the objective was to improve clinical management so that patients did not die because of mistakes or shortcomings in treatment and to ensure that district and upazila-level doctors were prepared if hospital admissions continued to rise.
The pressure is already visible in hospitals. Recent reporting from Dhaka found dedicated dengue wards and corners at some facilities full, forcing patients to be accommodated elsewhere as the caseload increased.
At a dengue awareness program in Mugda on Saturday, State Minister Habibur Rashid Habib called for greater public participation alongside city corporation operations, urging residents to regularly remove stagnant water and keep their homes and surroundings clean.
Despite the intensified response, health authorities cannot say when the outbreak will begin to subside.
Md Halimur Rashid, director of the Disease Control Division at DGHS, said dengue-control activities were being pursued at the highest levels of government, but the disease remained heavily influenced by rainfall, temperature and other environmental conditions.
As a result, he said, authorities could not provide a fixed timeframe for bringing the situation under control.
Bangladesh is still well below the catastrophic levels recorded during the 2023 epidemic, when 321,179 people were hospitalized and 1,705 died, the worst dengue outbreak in the country’s recorded history.
But this year’s trajectory is moving sharply in the wrong direction.
By Saturday, hospitalizations were already 74% higher than at the same point last year, deaths were up by about 27%, and more than half of the year’s patients had been recorded in September alone.
With another 4,749 hospitalizations in the first three days of October, the surge has now carried into a new month.

item.title: Uranium consignment reaches Rooppur nuclear power plant amid tight security
item.description:
Additional uranium fuel for the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant reached the project site on Saturday under tight security provided by the Army, Special Response Battalion (SRB) and police.
The convoy carrying the fuel arrived at the Rooppur project at around 12:20pm after travelling by road from Dhaka through Dashuria Mor in Ishwardi.
Project sources confirmed the arrival.
The fuel had reached Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 11:44pm on Friday, where officials of the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority received the shipment. Transportation to Rooppur began later that night under Army security.
Sources said three trucks carrying the uranium left the airport after 7am Saturday and travelled towards Rooppur via the Jamuna Bridge. Security was tightened in Ishwardi and Rooppur ahead of the shipment's arrival.
Project sources said 48 additional uranium fuel assemblies for the first unit and 163 for the second unit are expected to arrive in Bangladesh on nine flights during November-December.
Earlier, fuel brought for the first unit in 2023 was loaded into the reactor in May this year.
Dr Zaedul Hasan, managing director of Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited, said testing of the first unit's 16-megapascal high-pressure pressure-operated relief valve had been completed successfully.
During the test, the functionality of the control valves was verified, followed by checks of the main safety valve's response, opening and closing operations, alarms and related process parameters, he said.
Ishwardi Circle Additional Superintendent of Police Pranab Kumar said the uranium shipment reached Rooppur safely under strict security provided by the Army, SRB and police.
If preparations proceed as planned, the first unit is expected to supply 300 megawatts, or around 30 percent of the plant's total electricity generation capacity, to the national grid during November-December.

item.title: Milon: Substandard textbook suppliers to face punishment
item.description:
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon has warned that those involved in supplying substandard textbooks will face exemplary punishment.
He made the remarks as the chief guest at a programme titled “People’s Thoughts on Kachua’s Development”, organised by the Kachua Upazila Samity in Dhaka on Saturday.
Milon said there would be no compromise on textbook quality, adding that substandard books identified so far had been rejected and destroyed.
“Those involved in supplying substandard books will face exemplary punishment,” he said.
The minister said no concession would be made on the quality of textbook printing, whether in terms of paper, ink or printing presses.
He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman wanted to develop the country’s domestic printing industry. As part of that effort, no foreign company had been given textbook printing contracts this year, he added.
Milon expressed hope that quality textbooks would continue to be printed and supplied on time, as had been done in previous years.
The minister said a midday meal programme is currently being implemented in primary schools in 150 upazilas and would eventually be expanded across the country.
The government also plans to introduce a coupon system under the programme, allowing students to purchase meals from school canteens using coupons, he said.
New food items will be added to the menu, while food supply will be decentralised to boost local economies and encourage local entrepreneurs, Milon said. The initiative will initially be piloted in several districts before being rolled out nationwide.
Milon said sports and cultural studies books would be introduced in Class IV, while a new curriculum is being prepared with greater emphasis on technical education.
“There is no alternative to developing skilled human resources in the changing global landscape,” he said.
The government plans to establish technical schools and colleges in every upazila, he said, adding that a third language would also be introduced at these institutions.
Technical schools and colleges would also be established in Saudi Arabia, he added.
The minister said question papers for future examinations would be prepared separately at the Bangladesh Government Press (BG Press) and the Army Security Printing Press.
Examinations would be held on schedule to prevent students from losing valuable time due to delays, while efforts would also be made to avoid disruptions caused by monsoon-related disasters, he said.
Regarding the re-evaluation of examination scripts, Milon said the process had been revised based on practical considerations.
The government is also working to introduce a “cross-border education system” to establish Bangladesh as an “education hub,” he said. Milon said the university law would be amended to allow foreign educational institutions ranked among the world’s top 500 to open branches in Bangladesh, subject to approval.
He urged people in Kachua to give the highest priority to education for the area’s overall development.
“There is no alternative to technical and production-oriented education to develop a skilled workforce,” he said, adding that greater emphasis had been placed on technical education to help Kachua’s students become skilled human resources.

Govt employees to get 3 months’ salary arrears with October pay, calculation starts tomorrow
item.description:
Government officials and employees will receive nearly three months’ salary arrears in one payment under the new pay structure. However, how much each person will receive will depend on their new pay fixation.

The process will begin tomorrow, Monday. The Finance Division of the Ministry of Finance has asked that the process be completed by 20 October, according to Finance Division sources.

The new salaries of government employees will be fixed through the pay fixation module of iBAS++. Employees will log into the portal and provide their employment-related information.

They will first have to enter their personal details, including their national identity card information, date of birth, current position and grade, date of joining the service and current basic salary. They will also have to cross-check information from their previous pay fixation.

How much will govt employees’ salaries increase in 3 phases?

The basic salary for each employee under the new structure will be determined through the pay fixation process. Arrears will be calculated based on the difference between the new and previous salaries and the effective date.

According to Finance Division sources, once pay fixation is completed, the government will pay three months’ arrears in a lump sum. However, the amount will not be the same for everyone. The amount of arrears will depend on the employee’s grade, current basic salary, salary fixed under the new structure and the date on which the new salary takes effect.

Employees who have received promotions, transfers, time scales, selection grades or higher grades will also have to provide those details. They will need to keep the relevant office orders and necessary documents ready as proof.

In particular, names, NID numbers, dates of birth, designations, grades and salary-related information should be checked carefully. Incorrect or incomplete information could create complications in the pay fixation process.

The mobile phone number registered with iBAS++ will be required. Those who do not have an NID will have to apply after updating their date of birth and other information recorded in their service documents.

After 11 years, the government issued a gazette notification on 19 September to implement a new national pay structure for government employees. Under the new structure, the minimum basic salary has been set at Tk 20,000 and the maximum at Tk 156,000.

Salaries and allowances will be provided in phases over the 2026–27 and 2027–28 financial years. The first phase of the basic salary will cover 1 July to 31 December 2026, the second phase 1 January to 30 June 2027, and the third phase 1 July to 31 December 2027. Allowances will take effect from 1 January 2028.

According to the gazette notification, salaries under the new structure will be fixed based on the basic salary as of 30 June 2026. Forty per cent of the difference between the new and old basic salaries will be paid from 1 July to 31 December this year.

From 1 January to 30 June 2027, 70 per cent of the difference will be paid. From 1 July 2027, the full new basic salary will take effect. According to Finance Division sources, Tk 370 billion has been allocated in the current financial year to pay 70 per cent of the basic salary difference in two instalments.

The new pay scale brings relief and risks

Accounts offices to verify information

After an employee submits their information online, the relevant accounts office will verify it. If any discrepancies are found between the information and supporting documents, corrections may be required.

In other words, simply filling in the information online will not complete the process. The new information must match the employee’s previous service history and pay fixation records. If employees face problems submitting information online, they will be able to seek assistance from the relevant accounts officer.

Once pay fixation is finalised salary bills will be prepared based on the new basic salary. At the same time, the amount of arrears due will also be finalised.

To ensure that pay fixation is completed smoothly, online training is being provided to officials of accounts offices. iBAS++ is providing the training under the Finance Division’s ‘Strengthening Public Financial Management to Enable Service Delivery’ programme (SPFMS).

Relevant officials and employees from the offices of the Chief Accounts and Finance Officer (CAFO), Divisional Controller of Accounts (DCA), District Accounts and Finance Officer (DAFO) and Upazila Accounts Officer (UAO) are taking part in the training.

New recruits to receive bigger pay rises, different calculation for existing employees

Complications over calculations under new structure

Under the new pay order, a permanent employee who completes eight years in the same post without promotion and whose service is satisfactory will receive the next higher grade. After receiving the first higher grade, they will be eligible for a second higher grade after completing another six years in the same post.

However, officials of the Finance Division say there are complications in calculating salaries under the new structure for employees who received a time scale, selection grade or higher grade under the previous pay structure. These issues are being resolved.

According to a Finance Division order, if an employee received two or more selection grades, time scales or higher grades in the same post under the previous pay structure, they will no longer be eligible for a higher grade in that post under the new pay structure.

On the other hand, if an employee had received only one higher scale or grade in the same post as of 30 June 2026, they will be eligible for a second higher grade after completing the next six years.

Finance Division sources say that during pay fixation from 5 to 20 October, employees’ previous promotions, higher grades and pay fixation history must be properly verified alongside their current salary. Only when these records are accurate will it be possible to correctly calculate the new salary and arrears due.

LPG 12kg cylinder price rises by Tk 252
item.description:
The price of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplied by the private sector has increased at the consumer level. This time, the price has risen by Tk 21 per kilogramme.

As a result, the price of the most widely used 12kg LPG cylinder has increased by Tk 252, taking the new price to Tk 1,837 from Tk 1,585. The price had fallen by Tk 13 last month.

The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) announced the new price today, Sunday. The new price will take effect from 6:00 pm today. LPG prices rose in the wake of the outbreak of war in the Middle East.

LPG shortage as imports fall, prices rise

Following the start of a ceasefire, LPG prices began to decline on the international market. Prices had fluctuated over the past two months, but a significant surge has occurred again this month.

However, LPG supply in the market has remained below demand for the past three weeks. As a result, there have been allegations that 12kg LPG cylinders are being sold at Tk 500 to Tk 800 above the official price.

Earlier, LPG prices on the international market rose after the war spread across the Middle East. In April, the country recorded its highest-ever increase in LPG prices.

At the beginning of April, the price of a 12kg LPG cylinder was increased by Tk 387. It was raised by another Tk 212 on 19 April. However, prices fell for two consecutive months in June and July.

LPG import: BPC fails even after 7 months

According to BERC, LPG cylinders of various sizes are available in the market. From now on, the price of LPG will be Tk 153.06 per kilogramme. The prices of LPG cylinders of different sizes will be determined accordingly. Previously, the price was Tk 132.12 per kilogramme.

The commission determines LPG prices every month. However, LPG is not being sold in the market at the officially set prices. The 12kg LPG cylinder is the most widely used for household purposes.

There have been allegations that LPG sellers are charging customers more than the official price for each cylinder. Many people are turning to LPG cylinders for cooking at home amid the gas shortage.

The price of 12.5kg LPG cylinders supplied by state-owned companies has been kept unchanged at Tk 825. Meanwhile, the price of LPG used in vehicles, known as auto gas, has been set at Tk 84.62 per litre. Previously, it was Tk 73.09 per litre.

BERC has been setting LPG prices since April 2021. Propane and butane, the main components used to produce LPG, are imported from various countries. Every month, Saudi Arabian company Aramco publishes the prices of these two LPG components. This is known as the Saudi Contract Price (CP).

BERC adjusts LPG prices in Bangladesh based on this Saudi CP as the benchmark price. The commission calculates the average US dollar exchange rate for the entire month based on the invoice prices submitted by importing companies.

item.title: Govt targets NPL recovery with new Distressed Asset Law
item.description:
The government is formulating a new legal framework titled the Distressed Asset Management Act, 2026 to accelerate the recovery of non-performing loans (NPLs) and manage long-stagnant assets in banks and non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs).
Stakeholder feedback on the draft has already been collected.
If a borrower fails to clear dues within a stipulated timeframe, specialized asset management companies will be empowered to seize and sell mortgaged collateral.
These entities can also purchase defaulted loans and distressed assets, restructure or securitize them, and assume operational control of defaulting businesses.
While finance ministry officials expect the framework to establish a specialized ecosystem for bad-asset resolution, economists warn that systemic challenges remain.
A substantial portion of defaulted loans lacks adequate collateral, while other securities are inflated up to four to five times their actual market value—making actual recovery difficult even after asset transfers.
A separate regulatory body—the Distressed Asset Management Unit (Damu)—will be set up in Dhaka under the administrative supervision of Bangladesh Bank, operating with functional autonomy.
To operate, DAMCs must be registered under the Companies Act, 1994, meet cash-paid-up capital requirements set by Damu, maintain strict "fit and proper" management standards, and ensure at least 20% independent directors on their boards.
DAMCs can purchase bad debts directly from financial institutions via bilateral contracts, paying the agreed purchase price entirely in cash.
DAMCs may raise funds locally or internationally by issuing shares, bonds, debentures, and security certificates, or through joint ventures with eligible institutional investors.
DAMCs can negotiate settlements, take physical possession of mortgaged assets, lease or sell property, convert debt into equity, and assume control of defaulting firms.
They can also extend loan tenures, reduce or waive interest, and haircut principal amounts (subject to Damu approval for major write-downs). Settled borrowers will receive "no-dues certificates."
Collateral market value will be assessed by Bangladesh Bank-approved valuers to determine a reserve price.
Borrowers will receive a 60-day notice to clear dues or redeem assets at the reserve price.
Failing this, assets will be sold via public tenders, open auctions, or bilateral agreements at or above the reserve price (or re-auctioned at up to a 10% discount if initial bids fall short).
If a borrower refuses to yield physical possession, District Magistrates or designated Executive Magistrates must enforce eviction and hand over assets within 15 working days.
Distressed assets can be placed into special-purpose trusts, insulating them from the general creditors of the DAMC or the selling financial institution.
Trust claims will hold first charge and priority over all debts, including government taxes and duties.
DAMCs and banks can hire licensed loan servicer companies to assist in borrower contact, restructuring, and asset tracing.
Servicers are strictly prohibited from taking deposits, conducting banking, or using coercive/illegal recovery tactics.
Restrictions and penalties
Defaulting borrowers and affiliated individuals are strictly barred from holding ownership, management, or board roles in DAMUS, DAMCs, or loan servicers, and cannot participate in asset auctions.

item.title: North Korea’s Kim oversaw launch of missile that uses AI
item.description:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch of a missile, which allegedly used artificial intelligence to adjust its trajectory, state media reported on Sunday.
The AI technology means the missile is “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude”, Kim’s powerful sister had said, adding this meant there was “no way to avoid” an attack.
It launched from an area around the eastern coastal city of Wonsan early Saturday morning and flew more than 700 kilometres , South Korea’s military said.
“Through today’s launching drill, the strategic missile soldiers have fully demonstrated their professional qualifications and counterattack posture,” Kim said after the launch, according to an English-language dispatch by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
“We must continue our responsible efforts nonstop to constantly and repeatedly make the enemy recognize the reliability and fatality of our strategic offensive means,” he added.
Seoul’s military disputed Kim’s sister’s remarks that there would be “no way to avoid” the projectile guided by AI, saying the missile launched on Saturday could have been intercepted.
“South Korea and the United States maintain a firm combined defence posture and assess that the missile recently launched by North Korea was well within the detection and interception capabilities of the defencive assets operated by the two allies,” Seoul’s defence ministry said in a statement.
“We urge North Korea to immediately cease actions that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula,” it said, adding that the launch violated UN Security Council resolutions.
The KCNA report disclosed the exact coordinates where the missile hit its target, a level of detail analysts said reflected Pyongyang’s “confidence”.
“This time, the North disclosed the coordinates down to decimal points -- equivalent to a precision of roughly 30 centimetres,” Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP.
“It shows Kim’s stance that there is nothing to hide and an expression of confidence.”
Photos released by KCNA showed a missile soaring into the sky in a burst of orange flame.
Another photo showed Kim smiling, flanked by his daughter Ju Ae and wife Ri Sol Ju, who is seen clapping her hands in celebration.
Ju Ae, who was first introduced to the public in 2022, is the most likely successor to her father, according to South Korea’s spy agency, citing her increasingly prominent role at major state and military events.
The launch was conducted to help train soldiers operating the “hypersonic strategic weapon system”, KCNA reported.

item.title: Imported fruits becoming a luxury in Bangladesh
item.description:
In Dhaka's market, the price of one kilogram of sweet orange (Malta) is currently Tk520 to Tk550.
During the same period, it sells for Tk100 to Tk160 in India, Tk80 to Tk130 in Pakistan, Tk130 to Tk180 in Nepal, and Tk300 to Tk400 in Sri Lanka.
This means the price of this fruit in Bangladesh is up to seven times higher than in neighboring countries.
This extreme price disparity is not limited to sweet oranges; a report by the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission highlights similar trends across various imported foreign fruits, including apples, oranges, grapes, and dates.
The report states that high customs duties, valuation at inflated prices during assessment, hyper-profit-seeking cartels among sellers, and the classification of fruit as a luxury item are driving foreign imported fruits to sell at abnormally high prices in the country.
Consequently, these fruits have slipped beyond the reach of ordinary consumers. Once regarded as essential diet for patients, these fruits have now become a heavy burden on consumers.
The report reveals that while apples sell for Tk350 to Tk450 per kg in the domestic market, the price per kg in India is only Tk220. In Pakistan, it is Tk170; in Nepal, Tk240; and in Sri Lanka, a maximum of Tk450.
A similar pattern was observed in the prices of oranges, grapes, and dates.
According to business sources and the government report, although fruit has played a key role in meeting essential nutritional needs for years, it was classified as a luxury product about two years ago.
High import taxes were subsequently imposed as a result.
Furthermore, Customs assesses duties based on values higher than the actual booking prices in the international market.
On the other hand, the market offers room for monopolistic practices. A limited group of importers handles these shipments, leaving the market reliant on them.
There is a widespread tendency among importers, wholesalers, and retailers to seek excessive profit margins when selling fruit.
Official categorizing
It is reported that in early September 2024, a circular issued by the Policy and Regulation Department of Bangladesh Bank categorized these fruits under luxury goods.
At the same time, it instructed imports to be conducted with a 100% margin requirement to protect the domestic fruit market. From that point on, fruit prices began to rise unchecked.
The Tariff Commission states that currently, import duties ranging from 96.10% to 121.78% are imposed on these fruit imports.
These include Customs Duty (CD), Supplementary Duty (SD), Value Added Tax (VAT), Advance Income Tax (AIT), Regulatory Duty (RD), and Advance Tax (AT).
In effect, almost every type of tax imaginable is levied on fruit imports.
Arbitrary valuation during assessment has further aggravated the crisis.
Considering urgent public health needs, Bangladesh Bank issued a circular in the middle of last month waiving the 100% margin reservation requirement for these fruit importers. However, heavy tariff rates on these items remain in force.
To resolve this situation, the Tariff Commission recommended several measures. Chief among them is the rationalization of the tariff structure.
The commission suggests removing fresh fruit and dates from the luxury goods list, reclassifying them as essential commodities, and withdrawing regulatory and supplementary duties.
Additionally, it recommended assessing customs valuation in line with international market rates and expediting clearance through a "Green Channel" due to the perishable nature of fresh fruit.
The commission also recommended easing LC (Letter of Credit) facilities for small and medium traders and expanding cold storage coverage.
Meanwhile, on Saturday (October 3), Commerce Minister Khondokar Abdul Muqtadir held an exchange-of-views meeting with traders and representatives of relevant government agencies to ensure adequate fruit supply and stabilize market prices.
Expressing dissatisfaction over the prices of imported fruits, including sweet oranges, he demanded an explanation from fruit traders on how the retail price per kilogram of sweet orange reaches Tk520 even after accounting for import costs, duties, taxes, and other expenses.
During the meeting, traders cited supply shortages.
They noted that high duties, transportation costs, shipping and port complications, and losses from previous shipments led many traders to reduce sweet orange imports. They added that as perishable goods, these fruits carry significant financial risks during transit and storage.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, a leader from the Bangladesh Fresh Fruits Importers Association told Dhaka Tribune that the government's calculations exist only on paper. We are facing actual losses in real business.
Furthermore, high profit-seeking is rampant not just at the import level, but among wholesalers and retailers as well—something the government has failed to control through proper market monitoring, he added.
SM Nazer Hossain, vice president of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told the media that some traders take advantage of dengue outbreaks to create artificial shortages and inflate fruit prices. Fruit prices systematically spike at this time of year when diseases peak, becoming a recurring pattern.
He noted that although the government reduced duties on fresh fruit imports as recently as March, prices rose instead of falling.
He urged the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and other relevant agencies to enforce strict oversight.

item.title: Envoy: EU sees Bangladesh as growing strategic partner
item.description:
The European Union views Bangladesh as a partner of growing strategic importance and wants to elevate ties beyond the traditional donor-recipient relationship, its ambassador said on Sunday.
Speaking at the Bay of Bengal Conversation in the capital, the Ambassador and Head of the EU Delegation to Bangladesh, Michael Miller, said the bloc was looking at Bangladesh with a "different level of ambition" British High Commissioner to Bangladesh Sarah Cook on Sunday met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and discussed the overall state of Bangladesh-UK relations, including prospects for greater trade and investment, economic cooperation and human resource development.
The meeting was held at the Prime Minister’s Office in the Cabinet Division of the Bangladesh Secretariat, said a press release issued by the PM’s Press Wing.
During the meeting, they exchanged views on various issues of bilateral relations and matters of mutual interest.
They stressed the importance of further strengthening and broadening the longstanding and friendly relations between Bangladesh and the UK. The country approaches graduation from least developed country (LDC) status.
"We are looking at Bangladesh as a partner of growing strategic importance," he said while sharing his thoughts through the "Diplomatic Lens" at the international conference.
He described Bangladesh as a country of "scale, ambition and consequence", saying its importance extended across South Asia, the Bay of Bengal and the wider Indo-Pacific.
The envoy said the relationship was moving beyond the traditional donor-recipient framework that had characterized an important part of Bangladesh-EU cooperation over the past decades.
He acknowledged the contribution of the EU's Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preference scheme to Bangladesh's development progress, including its role in expanding employment opportunities for millions of people, particularly women.
As Bangladesh prepares for LDC graduation, he said the EU was ready to work with Dhaka to ensure a smooth and successful transition while exploring the prospect of a future Free Trade Agreement (FTA).
The envoy said the offer to explore such an agreement with a country yet to graduate from LDC status was unprecedented for the European Union.
"The key message is: we are ready to match the level of speed and ambition demonstrated by Bangladesh," he said.
He, however, said the two sides would first have to determine whether sufficient common ground existed for a balanced, reciprocal and mutually beneficial agreement.
The ambassador stressed the importance of ensuring a level playing field for businesses under any future trade arrangement.
He said the success of deeper Bangladesh-EU economic engagement would depend on strong and accountable institutions, rule of law, labour rights, human rights, environmental protection and good governance. "These issues are central; they are not peripheral," he said.
The EU envoy said Bangladesh was navigating an important phase in its development journey amid LDC graduation, political transition, economic pressure, climate vulnerability and an increasingly complex external environment.
He said stronger institutions, independent oversight mechanisms and predictable and inclusive decision-making would help Bangladesh withstand geopolitical, geoeconomic, climate, social and technological pressures.
The ambassador also underlined the importance of constitutional reform, greater political consensus, skilled human resources, green growth, diversified exports and reliable infrastructure for the country's future development.
"If this country is to attract investment, both foreign and domestic, and to create meaningful jobs for its youth, it will require strong institutions and oversight mechanisms," he said.
He said critical infrastructure needed to be safeguarded while data management should remain transparent.
Highlighting the EU's investment approach, the envoy said European engagement sought to combine investment with technology, international standards, long-term capital and innovation.
He cited the Laldia Container Terminal in Chittagong and green bond initiatives as examples of areas where European engagement could bring additional value.
The ambassador said the EU could also share its experience in public administration and political and economic transition with Bangladesh.
He said Europe itself had gone through major transformations from autocratic systems towards democratic governance and modern economic institutions.
The EU, he said, wanted to help Bangladesh navigate increasing global competition while remaining "open, sovereign, resilient and connected".
Earlier in his speech, the envoy said the EU's own response to growing global uncertainty had been to strengthen its strategic autonomy while remaining open, cooperative and committed to international law and multilateralism.
He said the EU sought partnerships based on mutual interest, respect, fairness and a level playing field, while offering rules-based trade, sustainable investment and cooperation in climate, connectivity, digital transformation and human development.
The Bay of Bengal Conversation is being held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in Dhaka.
